slides.say: Two buses leave a station together at six forty. Line five leaves every sixteen minutes, and line nine leaves every twenty minutes. Counting six forty as the first time they leave together, when do they leave together for the fourth time?
So two schedules repeat, and we look for the times they meet. [short pause] We'll solve it in two different ways, by listing both schedules, and then with a common multiple.
[short pause] Let's start by listing, neatly. Line five leaves every sixteen minutes. Six forty, six fifty-six, seven twelve, seven twenty-eight, seven forty-four, and eight o'clock.
Line nine leaves every twenty minutes. Six forty, seven o'clock, seven twenty, seven forty, and eight o'clock.

So they meet again at eight o'clock. From six forty to eight o'clock is an hour and twenty minutes, eighty minutes. And at eight o'clock both start together again, so the same thing repeats. They meet every eighty minutes.

Now careful with the count. Six forty is already the first time. Four times have only three gaps between them. So eight o'clock is the second time, nine twenty is the third, and ten forty is the fourth. This idea comes back a lot. Ten posts in a row have only nine gaps between them. So when you count times or items, count the gaps separately.
at: Four times have only three gaps

slides.say: Nine twenty is the trap, because that's only the third time. Choice number three is our answer. But listing every match takes a long time, so let's see a faster way.
at: Choice number three is our answer

slides.say: [pause] Now with a common multiple. When do two repeating things meet again? After a number of minutes that divides both by sixteen and by twenty.

The easy way is to take the bigger gap, twenty, and jump by it. We get twenty, forty, sixty and eighty. Twenty, forty and sixty don't divide by sixteen. Eighty is five times sixteen, so eighty divides by both sixteen and twenty.

slides: Why the bigger one? Because it takes fewer jumps. Jumping by sixteen, we'd need five jumps to reach eighty. Jumping by twenty, only four.

slides.say: So they leave together every eighty minutes, and the fourth time is three gaps after six forty. Eighty minutes is an hour and twenty minutes. Six forty plus an hour and twenty is eight o'clock, then nine twenty, then ten forty. Choice number three is our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
at: Choice number three is our answer
